detail: 'Stays readable' is not asserted in a way that can fail: a cell that breaks after every letter still has no horizontal scroll, sits inside the viewport, has scrollWidth <= clientWidth and its full textContent. The only data is one unbreakable 58-letter city, so the case never shows that ordinary values wrap only between words. Add an order shipping to 'Redmond, U.S.' and assert at 375x667 that its .order-ships-to is as wide as its row (within 1px) and renders on one line (height not above 1.5x the computed line-height). For the long-city order, assert the cell is as wide as its row and 'United Kingdom' is not broken mid-word.

The assertions prove that text fits without clipping, but a one-character-wide cell wrapping after every letter satisfies all of them. Add a 375px check using Redmond, U.S. and assert that the rendered destination occupies at most two lines, as required by the upheld ui-ships-to-375-unreadable finding. Keep the long-word overflow check.

The recorded response shows Redmond/U.S. as order 10 and Paris/France as order 1, contradicting the case's lower-number/higher-number expectations. The test correlates each order using the newly added ID instead. Correct the plan to record each POST's added orderNumber and assert destinations by those IDs, as TC-SHIP-1-04 does; numeric ordering cannot identify creation order here.

The case requires date to be no later than the GET time, but the assertion accepts getTime + 1000 milliseconds. A future timestamp within that extra second passes. Enforce the specified upper bound or obtain an explicit clock-tolerance requirement in the plan.

The test accepts any status later in STATUS_SEQUENCE without checking that the order actually reached it. For a recorded Submitted order, a UI incorrectly displaying Paid, Shipped or Cancelled passes. When the displayed status differs, verify it against the real order state through the API.
